'''Mary-Dell Chilton''' (February 2, 1939 – June 24, 2026) was an American biochemist, inventor and writer who was one of the founders of modern plant [[biotechnology]]. She performed research at [[Washington University in St. Louis]] and was a Distinguished Science Fellow at [[Syngenta]] Biotechnology, Inc. Chilton was notable for her discovery of the presence of ''[[Agrobacterium]]'' [[Ti plasmid]] [[DNA]] fragments in the nuclear DNA of crown [[gall]] tissue in 1977.<ref name=obit/>

During her career, she was awarded the [[World Food Prize]] (2013) and the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]] by President [[Joe Biden]] in 2023. She was also inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]].

==Early life and education==
Chilton was born in [[Indianapolis]], Indiana on February 2, 1939.<ref name=obit/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lib.ncsu.edu/findingaids/mc00376|title=Mary-Dell Chilton Papers 1947–1999|publisher=Lib.NCSU.edu|accessdate=June 26, 2026|archive-date=July 13, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713140809/https://www.lib.ncsu.edu/findingaids/mc00376|url-status=live}}</ref> She was raised by her grandmother in [[Southern Pines, North Carolina]].<ref name=obit/>

Chilton attended private school for her early education.<ref name=Stanley>{{cite book |last=Stanley |first=Autumn |date=1993 |title=Mothers and Daughters of Invention: Notes for a Revised History of Technology |url=https://archive.org/details/mothersdaughters00stan/page/83 |location=New Brunswick, N.J. |publisher=Rutgers University Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/mothersdaughters00stan/page/83 83] |isbn=978-0813521978}}</ref> She earned both a B.S. and Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]].<ref name=Locke>{{cite news|last1=Locke |first1=Mandy |title=2013 Tar Heel of the Year: Mary-Dell Chilton Is Changing the Way the World Eats |url=http://www.newsobserver.com/2013/12/28/3489825/2013-tar-heel-of-the-year-mary.html |access-date=June 27, 2014 |publisher=The News & Observer |date=December 28, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140218005535/http://www.newsobserver.com/2013/12/28/3489825/2013-tar-heel-of-the-year-mary.html |archive-date=February 18, 2014 }}</ref> She later completed postdoctoral work at the [[University of Washington]] in Seattle.<ref name=Stanley />

==Career and research==
Chilton taught and performed research at [[Washington University in St. Louis]].<ref name=Stanley /> While on faculty there in the late 1970s and early 1980s, she led a collaborative research study that produced the first transgenic plants.<ref name=obit/> Her scientific achievements, Chilton was noted for work that led to the first genetically modified plants which contributed to the development of pest resistance and drought tolerance.<ref name=obit2/>

In 1977, Chilton was the first to demonstrate the presence of a fragment of ''[[Agrobacterium]]'' [[Ti plasmid]] [[DNA]] in the nuclear DNA of crown [[gall]] tissue. Her research on ''Agrobacterium'' also showed that the [[gene]]s responsible for causing disease could be removed from the bacterium without adversely affecting its ability to insert its own DNA into plant cells and modify the plant's [[genome]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/295432a0| title = Agrobacterium rhizogenes inserts T-DNA into the genomes of the host plant root cells| journal = Nature| volume = 295| issue = 5848| pages = 432| year = 1982| last1 = Chilton | first1 = M. D. | last2 = Tepfer | first2 = D. A. | last3 = Petit | first3 = A. | last4 = David | first4 = C. | last5 = Casse-Delbart | first5 = F. | last6 = Tempé | first6 = J. | bibcode = 1982Natur.295..432C| s2cid = 4354924}}</ref> Chilton described what she had done as ''disarming'' the bacterial [[plasmid]] responsible for the DNA transfer. She and her collaborators produced the first [[genetically modified]] plants using ''Agrobacterium'' carrying the disarmed Ti plasmid (1983). She has been called the "queen of ''Agrobacterium''."<ref>{{cite book|last=Charles|first=Daniel|title=Lords of the Harvest: Biotech, Big Money, and the Future of Food |year=2001|publisher=The Perseus Books Group|location=Reading, MA|isbn=9780738202914|url=https://archive.org/details/lordsofharvestbi00char}}</ref>

After her breakthroughs in the 1980s, Chilton moved to the private sector at [[Syngenta|Syngenta Biotechnology]] in [[Research Triangle Park]], eventually becoming vice president of agricultural biotechnology and principal scientist.<ref name=obit/> Chilton was author of more than 100 scientific publications. She was a Distinguished Science Fellow at Syngenta. She also worked with [[CIBA-Geigy]] Corporation, a legacy company of Syngenta.<ref name=obit/>

==Personal life and death==
Chilton was an avid canoer, with her last trip going through [[Stillwater Canyon]] in [[Utah]] at age 76.<ref name=obit/> She had two sons, Mark and Andrew.<ref name=obit/>

Chilton died at her home in [[Carrboro, North Carolina]], on June 24, 2026, at the age of 87.<ref name=obit>{{cite web|url=https://www.newsobserver.com/news/local/article316284312.html|title=Mary-Dell Chilton, NC biochemist who revolutionized agriculture, dies at 87|publisher=News Observer|accessdate=June 26, 2026|date=June 26, 2026}}</ref><ref name=obit2>{{cite web|url=https://hoodline.com/2026/06/carrboro-biotech-trailblazer-mary-dell-chilton-who-rewired-crop-dna-dies-at-87/|title=Carrboro Biotech Trailblazer Mary-Dell Chilton, Who Rewired Crop DNA, Dies At 87|publisher=Hoodline|date=June 26, 2026|accessdate=June 26, 2026|archive-date=June 26, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260626223552/https://hoodline.com/2026/06/carrboro-biotech-trailblazer-mary-dell-chilton-who-rewired-crop-dna-dies-at-87/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Chilton hall of heroes.jpg|thumb|Chilton with U.S. Agriculture Secretary [[Tom Vilsack]] in 2015]]

For her work with ''[[Agrobacterium tumefaciens]]'', Chilton was recognized with an honorary doctorate from the University of Louvaine, the [[John Scott Medal]] from the City of Philadelphia, membership in the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]], and the [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Benjamin Franklin Medal]] in Life Sciences from the [[Franklin Institute]].<ref name=obit/>

Chilton was honored by the [[Crop Science Society of America]] in 2011 with the organization's Presidential Award.<ref>{{cite web|title=Crop Science Society of America Announces 2011 Award Recipients|url=https://www.newswise.com/articles/crop-science-society-of-america-announces-2011-award-recipients|publisher=Crop Science Society of America (CSSA)|access-date=April 28, 2013|archive-date=February 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203074342/https://www.newswise.com/articles/crop-science-society-of-america-announces-2011-award-recipients|url-status=live}}</ref> In honor of her many achievements, in 2002 Syngenta announced creation of the Mary-Dell Chilton Center – a new administrative and conference center which was added to the company's facility in [[Research Triangle Park]], in [[North Carolina]].<ref>{{cite web|title=SBI Founder and Distinguished Scientist: Mary-Dell Chilton PhD|url=http://www.syngentabiotech.com/biotech/mary_dell_chilton.aspx|publisher=Sygenta US: Biotechnology|access-date=April 28, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161129211020/http://www.syngentabiotech.com/biotech/mary_dell_chilton.aspx|archive-date=November 29, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In June 2013, she was named a laureate of the prestigious 2013 [[World Food Prize]].<ref>{{in lang|fr}} Catherine Morand, "Le prix mondial de l'alimentation à Monsanto et Syngenta ? Une farce", [[Le Temps|www.letemps.ch]], October 16, 2013 (page visited on October 16, 2013).</ref><ref>[http://www.heraldonline.com/2013/06/19/4960636/syngentas-mary-dell-chilton-named.html Syngenta's Mary-Dell Chilton named 2013 World Food Prize laureate]</ref><ref name=Pollack>{{cite news|last1=Pollack|first1=Andrew|title=Executive at Monsanto Wins Global Food Honor|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/06/20/business/monsanto-executive-is-among-world-food-prize-winners.html |access-date=June 27, 2014|work=The New York Times|date=June 19, 2013|archive-date=May 19, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190519222514/https://www.nytimes.com/2013/06/20/business/monsanto-executive-is-among-world-food-prize-winners.html |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2015, Chilton was elected to the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]].<ref name=NIHoF>{{cite web|url=https://www.invent.org/inductees/mary-dell-chilton|title=Mary-Dell Chilton|publisher=National Inventors Hall of Fame|access-date=February 7, 2015|archive-date=June 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200620180543/https://www.invent.org/inductees/mary-dell-chilton|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2020, she was one of eight women featured in "The Only One in the Room" display at the [[Smithsonian Institution|Smithsonian]] [[National Museum of American History]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 11, 2020|title=Mary-Dell Chilton|url=https://americanhistory.si.edu/american-enterprise/new-perspectives/only-one-room/mary-dell-chilton|access-date=July 25, 2020|website=National Museum of American History|language=en|archive-date=November 8, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231108115908/https://americanhistory.si.edu/american-enterprise/new-perspectives/only-one-room/mary-dell-chilton|url-status=dead}}</ref> Chilton was recognized as a Pioneer Member of the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://aspb.org/membership/aspb-pioneer-members/ | title=ASPB Pioneer Members | access-date=October 17, 2022 | archive-date=October 17, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017071720/https://aspb.org/membership/aspb-pioneer-members/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2023, US President [[Joe Biden]] awarded Chilton the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]].<ref>{{Cite press release |title=President Biden Honors Leading American Scientists, Technologists, and Innovators |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/10/24/president-biden-honors-leading-american-scientists-technologists-and-innovators/ |publisher=The White House |date=October 24, 2023 |access-date=October 25, 2023 |language=en-US}}</ref>
